title: How to Disagree
paragraphs_en: March 2008

The web is turning writing into a conversation. Twenty years ago, writers wrote and readers read. The web lets readers respond, and increasingly they do --in comment threads, on forums, and in their own blog posts.

Many who respond to something disagree with it. That's to be expected. Agreeing tends to motivate people less than disagreeing. And when you agree there's less to say. You could expand on something the author said, but he has probably already explored the most interesting implications. When you disagree you're entering territory he may not have explored.

The result is there's a lot more disagreeing going on, especially measured by the word. That doesn't mean people are getting angrier. The structural change in the way we communicate is enough to account for it. But though it's not anger that's driving the increase in disagreement, there's a danger that the increase in disagreement will make people angrier. Particularly online, where it's easy to say things you'd never say face to face.

If we're all going to be disagreeing more, we should be careful to do it well. What does it mean to disagree well? Most readers can tell the difference between mere name-calling and a carefully reasoned refutation, but I think it would help to put names on the intermediate stages. So here's an attempt at a disagreement hierarchy:
DH0. Name-calling.
This is the lowest form of disagreement, and probably also the most common. We've all seen comments like this:
But it's important to realize that more articulate name-calling has just as little weight. A comment like
The author is a self-important dilettante.
The author is a self-important dilettante.
is really nothing more than a pretentious version of "u r a fag."
DH1. Ad Hominem.

An ad hominem attack is not quite as weak as mere name-calling. It might actually carry some weight. For example, if a senator wrote an article saying senators' salaries should be increased, one could respond:
Of course he would say that. He's a senator.
Of course he would say that. He's a senator.

This wouldn't refute the author's argument, but it may at least be relevant to the case. It's still a very weak form of disagreement, though. If there's something wrong with the senator's argument, you should say what it is; and if there isn't, what difference does it make that he's a senator?

Saying that an author lacks the authority to write about a topic is a variant of ad hominem--and a particularly useless sort, because good ideas often come from outsiders. The question is whether the author is correct or not. If his lack of authority caused him to make mistakes, point those out. And if it didn't, it's not a problem.
DH2. Responding to Tone.
The next level up we start to see responses to the writing, rather than the writer. The lowest form of these is to disagree with the author's tone. E.g.
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier > fashion.
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier > fashion.

Though better than attacking the author, this is still a weak form of disagreement. It matters much more whether the author is wrong or right than what his tone is. Especially since tone is so hard to judge. Someone who has a chip on their shoulder about some topic might be offended by a tone that to other readers seemed neutral.

So if the worst thing you can say about something is to criticize its tone, you're not saying much. Is the author flippant, but correct? Better that than grave and wrong. And if the author is incorrect somewhere, say where.
DH3. Contradiction.

In this stage we finally get responses to what was said, rather than how or by whom. The lowest form of response to an argument is simply to state the opposing case, with little or no supporting evidence.
This is often combined with DH2 statements, as in:
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier > fashion. Intelligent design is a legitimate scientific theory.
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier > fashion. Intelligent design is a legitimate scientific theory.
Contradiction can sometimes have some weight. Sometimes merely seeing the opposing case stated explicitly is enough to see that it's right. But usually evidence will help.
DH4. Counterargument.

At level 4 we reach the first form of convincing disagreement: counterargument. Forms up to this point can usually be ignored as proving nothing. Counterargument might prove something. The problem is, it's hard to say exactly what.

Counterargument is contradiction plus reasoning and/or evidence. When aimed squarely at the original argument, it can be convincing. But unfortunately it's common for counterarguments to be aimed at something slightly different. More often than not, two people arguing passionately about something are actually arguing about two different things. Sometimes they even agree with one another, but are so caught up in their squabble they don't realize it.

There could be a legitimate reason for arguing against something slightly different from what the original author said: when you feel they missed the heart of the matter. But when you do that, you should say explicitly you're doing it.
DH5. Refutation.

The most convincing form of disagreement is refutation. It's also the rarest, because it's the most work. Indeed, the disagreement hierarchy forms a kind of pyramid, in the sense that the higher you go the fewer instances you find.

To refute someone you probably have to quote them. You have to find a "smoking gun," a passage in whatever you disagree with that you feel is mistaken, and then explain why it's mistaken. If you can't find an actual quote to disagree with, you may be arguing with a straw man.

While refutation generally entails quoting, quoting doesn't necessarily imply refutation. Some writers quote parts of things they disagree with to give the appearance of legitimate refutation, then follow with a response as low as DH3 or even DH0.
DH6. Refuting the Central Point.
The force of a refutation depends on what you refute. The most powerful form of disagreement is to refute someone's central point.

Even as high as DH5 we still sometimes see deliberate dishonesty, as when someone picks out minor points of an argument and refutes those. Sometimes the spirit in which this is done makes it more of a sophisticated form of ad hominem than actual refutation. For example, correcting someone's grammar, or harping on minor mistakes in names or numbers. Unless the opposing argument actually depends on such things, the only purpose of correcting them is to discredit one's opponent.

Truly refuting something requires one to refute its central point, or at least one of them. And that means one has to commit explicitly to what the central point is. So a truly effective refutation would look like:
The author's main point seems to be x. As he says:
The author's main point seems to be x. As he says:
But this is wrong for the following reasons...
But this is wrong for the following reasons...
The quotation you point out as mistaken need not be the actual statement of the author's main point. It's enough to refute something it depends upon.
What It Means

Now we have a way of classifying forms of disagreement. What good is it? One thing the disagreement hierarchydoesn'tgive us is a way of picking a winner. DH levels merely describe the form of a statement, not whether it's correct. A DH6 response could still be completely mistaken.
But while DH levels don't set a lower bound on the convincingness of a reply, they do set an upper bound. A DH6 response might be unconvincing, but a DH2 or lower response is always unconvincing.

The most obvious advantage of classifying the forms of disagreement is that it will help people to evaluate what they read. In particular, it will help them to see through intellectually dishonest arguments. An eloquent speaker or writer can give the impression of vanquishing an opponent merely by using forceful words. In fact that is probably the defining quality of a demagogue. By giving names to the different forms of disagreement, we give critical readers a pin for popping such balloons.

Such labels may help writers too. Most intellectual dishonesty is unintentional. Someone arguing against the tone of something he disagrees with may believe he's really saying something. Zooming out and seeing his current position on the disagreement hierarchy may inspire him to try moving up to counterargument or refutation.

But the greatest benefit of disagreeing well is not just that it will make conversations better, but that it will make the people who have them happier. If you study conversations, you find there is a lot more meanness down in DH1 than up in DH6. You don't have to be mean when you have a real point to make. In fact, you don't want to. If you have something real to say, being mean just gets in the way.
If moving up the disagreement hierarchy makes people less mean, that will make most of them happier. Most people don't really enjoy being mean; they do it because they can't help it.

paragraphs_zh: 网络正在将写作变成一种对话。二十年前，作者写，读者读。网络让读者可以回应，而且越来越多的人确实在这样做——在评论区、论坛和他们自己的博客文章中。
许多回应者对所回应的内容持反对意见。这在意料之中。与赞同相比，反对更容易激发人们表达的欲望。而且当你赞同时，能说的也更少。你可以对作者说过的某些观点加以展开，但他可能已经探讨了最有趣的延伸。当你反对时，你进入的是他可能尚未探索的领域。
结果就是出现了更多的争论，尤其是从字数来衡量。这并不意味着人们变得更加愤怒。我们沟通方式的结构性变化足以解释这一点。但是，虽然推动争论增加的不是愤怒，但争论的增加却有使人们变得更加愤怒的危险。尤其是在网上，人们很容易说出面对面时绝不会说的话。
如果我们都将面临更多的争论，我们应该注意把它做好。好的争论意味着什么？大多数读者能分辨出单纯的谩骂和精心推理的反驳之间的区别，但我认为给中间阶段命名会有所帮助。所以这里是我对反驳层级的一个尝试：
DH0. 谩骂。
这是最低级的反驳形式，可能也是最常见的。我们都见过这样的评论：
但重要的是要认识到，更文雅的谩骂同样没有分量。像这样的评论
The author is a self-important dilettante.
The author is a self-important dilettante.
实际上不过是"u r a fag"的一个装腔作势的版本。
DH1. 人身攻击。
人身攻击不像单纯的谩骂那么软弱无力。它可能确实有一些分量。例如，如果一位参议员写了一篇文章说参议员的工资应该提高，有人可以回应：
Of course he would say that. He's a senator.
Of course he would say that. He's a senator.
这不会反驳作者的论点，但它至少可能与案件有关。不过，这仍然是一种非常弱的反驳形式。如果参议员的论点有什么问题，你应该说出问题是什么；如果没有问题，他是参议员又有什么关系呢？
说一个作者缺乏就某个话题写作的权威性，是人身攻击的一个变体——而且是一种特别无用的变体，因为好的想法往往来自局外人。问题在于作者是否正确。如果他缺乏权威性导致了错误，请指出那些错误。如果没有，那就不是问题。
DH2. 针对语气。
再上一层，我们开始看到针对文章本身的回应，而非针对作者。其中最低级的形式是对作者的语气表示不满。例如：
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier fashion.
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier fashion.
虽然比攻击作者本人要好，但这仍然是一种弱的反驳形式。作者是对还是错，比他的语气如何重要得多。尤其是因为语气很难判断。一个对某个话题耿耿于怀的人可能会被一种在其他读者看来很中立的语气所冒犯。
所以如果你能说出的最糟糕的事情只是批评某样东西的语气，那你其实没说什么实质内容。作者轻浮但正确？那也比严肃但错误要好。如果作者在某处不正确，请指出在哪里。
DH3. 矛盾对立。
在这个阶段，我们终于看到了对论点内容本身的回应，而非关于怎么说的或谁说的。对一个论点最低级的回应就是简单地陈述相反的立场，几乎不提供或完全不提供支持性证据。
这通常与DH2的陈述结合在一起，如：
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier fashion. Intelligent design is a legitimate scientific theory.
I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier fashion. Intelligent design is a legitimate scientific theory.
矛盾对立有时候也有一些分量。有时候仅仅看到对立的观点被明确陈述出来，就足以让人看到它是对的。但通常证据会更有帮助。
DH4. 反论证。
到了第四层，我们到达了第一种有说服力的反驳形式：反论证。在此之前的各种形式通常可以忽略不计，因为它们什么也证明不了。反论证可能确实能证明一些东西。问题是，很难说清楚它究竟证明了什么。
反论证是矛盾对立加上推理和/或证据。当它直接针对原始论点时，可以很有说服力。但不幸的是，反论证常常针对的是略有不同的东西。两个人激烈争论某件事，实际上往往是在争论两件不同的事情。有时候他们甚至彼此认同，但因为太投入于争吵而没有意识到。
针对与原作者所说的略有不同的东西进行反驳，可能有正当理由：当你觉得他们没有抓住问题的核心。但当你这样做时，你应该明确说明你在这样做。
DH5. 驳斥。
最有说服力的反驳形式是驳斥。它也是最罕见的，因为它需要最多的工作。事实上，反驳层级形成了一种金字塔结构，越往上走，你能找到的实例就越少。
要驳斥某人，你可能需要引用他们的话。你必须找到一个"确凿证据"，在你所反对的内容中找到一段你认为有误的文字，然后解释为什么它是错的。如果你找不到一段实际的引文来反对，你可能是在攻击一个稻草人。
虽然驳斥通常需要引用，但引用不一定意味着驳斥。有些作者引用他们反对内容的部分，营造出合理驳斥的假象，然后跟上的回应却低至DH3甚至DH0。
DH6. 驳斥核心论点。
驳斥的力量取决于你驳斥了什么。最有力的反驳形式是驳斥某人的核心论点。
即使在DH5的高度，我们有时仍会看到故意的不诚实行为，比如有人挑出论点中的次要细节来驳斥。有时候这样做的精神更像是一种精致的人身攻击，而非真正的驳斥。例如，纠正某人的语法，或纠缠于名字或数字中的小错误。除非对方的论点确实依赖于这些东西，否则纠正它们的唯一目的就是诋毁对手。
真正驳斥某样东西需要驳斥其核心论点，或至少其中之一。这意味着你必须明确指出核心论点是什么。所以一个真正有效的驳斥应该是这样的：
The author's main point seems to be x. As he says:
The author's main point seems to be x. As he says:
But this is wrong for the following reasons...
But this is wrong for the following reasons...
你指出有误的引文不必是作者核心论点的原文陈述。驳斥它所依赖的某个东西就足够了。
这意味着什么
现在我们有了一种分类反驳形式的方法。它有什么用呢？反驳层级没有给我们的一样东西是判定胜负的方法。DH级别仅仅描述了一个陈述的形式，而不是它是否正确。一个DH6级别的回应仍然可能完全错误。
但虽然DH级别没有为回应的说服力设定下限，它们确实设定了一个上限。DH6的回应可能不具说服力，但DH2或更低级别的回应总是不具说服力的。
对反驳形式进行分类最明显的好处是它将帮助人们评估他们所读到的内容。特别是，它将帮助他们看穿在智识上不诚实的论点。一个雄辩的演说家或作者可以仅仅通过使用有力的措辞就给人一种击败对手的印象。事实上，这可能正是煽动家的典型特征。通过给不同形式的反驳命名，我们给了审慎的读者一根戳破这类气球的针。
这些标签也可能对作者有所帮助。大多数智识上的不诚实是无意的。一个针对他所反对内容的语气进行反驳的人可能相信自己真的在说什么实质性的东西。退一步看看自己在反驳层级上的当前位置，可能会激励他尝试上升到反论证或驳斥的层次。
但是，好好争论的最大好处不仅在于它会使对话变得更好，还在于它会使参与对话的人更加快乐。如果你研究对话，你会发现在DH1层面的恶意远比DH6层面多得多。当你有真正的论点要阐述时，你不需要刻薄。事实上，你也不想刻薄。如果你有真正想说的东西，刻薄只会碍事。
如果在反驳层级上向上攀升能使人们不那么刻薄，那将使大多数人更快乐。大多数人并不真的喜欢刻薄；他们这样做是因为忍不住。
